title: When Science Meets the Unknown
subtitle: The Limits of Human Knowledge and the Endless Search for Understanding

sections.heading: 1. The More We Know, the Wider the Unknown Becomes
paragraphs: A boy is looking at a photograph of a distant galaxy on his father's phone.
“How long did the light take to get here?” he asks.
His father checks the distance and tries to explain what a light-year means. The boy studies the bright spiral on the screen for another moment.
“Then does it still look like that now?”

The father pauses. He has been about to answer with a number, but the second question asks for something the photograph cannot show. The image is not a window onto the galaxy as it exists at this instant. It is a record of light that began its journey long before the two of them were born. The sharper the photograph, the more striking the distance between seeing and knowing.

There was a time when people imagined the stars as lamps hung in a celestial ceiling, or as the dwellings of gods. Over centuries, observation and mathematics replaced many of those explanations. We learned that Earth travels around the Sun, that stars are other suns, and that some of the faint points above us belong to galaxies unimaginably far away.
Did knowledge make the night sky less mysterious?

In one sense, it made the sky less frightening. We can predict eclipses instead of treating them as sudden warnings. We can measure orbits and build spacecraft. But every instrument that extends our reach also reveals a new frontier. A better telescope does not bring the universe to an end. It shows us how much more there is to investigate.
This is not a failure of science. It is one of its great achievements: a method that lets an explanation become more precise—or be discarded—when new evidence demands it.

Science does not promise that human beings will eventually know everything. It asks us to offer explanations that can be examined, challenged, and revised. An answer earns trust not because it sounds complete, but because it survives careful testing—and remains open to correction.
The real danger begins when a provisional explanation is presented as an eternal certainty. Near the edge of what is known, intellectual humility is not weakness. It is part of the work.

sections.heading: 2. How the Ancients Looked at the World
paragraphs: Long before the rise of modern experimental science, people were trying to understand change. They watched the seasons, recorded celestial events, learned from harvests and illnesses, and struggled to make decisions amid political upheaval and family uncertainty. They did not have today's laboratories or statistical methods. They had observation, memory, analogy, ritual, argument, and the accumulated language of generations.

The *Yijing*, often called the *Book of Changes* or *I Ching* in English, belongs to that long history. The received text includes early materials associated with divination. Across later centuries, commentarial traditions developed ethical, cosmological, and philosophical interpretations. These layers should not be collapsed into the work of a single author or a single historical moment.
What might a contemporary reader gain from it?

Consider a family deciding whether to move to another country. They can calculate the cost of housing, compare job opportunities, and research schools. None of those calculations will fully capture the strain of leaving familiar people behind, or the possibility that the family's needs will change after arrival. Reading an old text about change might prompt a useful question: which parts of the plan can the family revise if circumstances shift? That question does not forecast the future or make the decision for them.

That distinction matters. A philosophical insight is not the same thing as a scientific discovery. The hexagrams of the *Yijing* are not equations in modern physics, and resemblance is not experimental confirmation. A resemblance between an ancient phrase and a modern scientific concept does not establish that the ancient text predicted the discovery. To make that claim responsibly, one would have to examine the original language, the date and history of the passage, and what its authors could reasonably have meant.
Respect for the past does not require us to credit earlier thinkers with experiments they never performed. Nor does respect for science require us to dismiss every old question as foolish.
The more generous—and more exacting—approach is to let historical texts speak from their own time. We can learn from them without pretending they knew what only later generations were able to test.

sections.heading: 3. What Science Can Tell Us—and What We Must Still Decide
paragraphs: How much weight can a bridge safely carry? Does a treatment improve outcomes compared with an appropriate control in a well-designed study? Under what conditions will a material fracture?
These are questions for measurement, controlled investigation, and evidence that other people can examine. A compelling story cannot substitute for a reliable test.
But suppose the bridge will connect a prosperous neighborhood to a poorer one. Who should pay for it? Whose homes might be displaced? Which benefits matter most, and who gets to decide?
Engineering can inform those choices. It cannot, by itself, settle every question of fairness.

The same is true in medicine. Research may show a benefit for a defined group of patients. We must still consider side effects, informed consent, access, cost, and the circumstances of the person receiving care. Facts are indispensable to ethical judgment; they do not remove the need for judgment.

Science and philosophy are not rival teams fighting over a single territory. Scientific inquiry depends on ideas about evidence, causation, explanation, and what counts as a good reason to believe something. Philosophy, in turn, becomes careless when it ignores what empirical research has established.

Artificial intelligence makes this relationship especially visible. A system may generate a convincing voice, produce a polished report, or recommend a course of action. The question of whether it can do so is partly technical. Whether it should be used in a particular situation raises questions about consent, privacy, accountability, and deception.
Technology may tell us how to build a stronger bridge. It cannot relieve us of responsibility for the people whose lives the bridge will change.

sections.heading: 4. The Origins of Life: Two Questions, Not One
paragraphs: A seed rests in dark soil. Given water, warmth, and the right conditions, it begins to grow. Its first shoot pushes upward, and a few days later a small green leaf unfolds.
We can study this process in extraordinary detail. We can investigate the seed's cells, the role of light and water, and the molecular machinery that makes growth possible.

Yet a different question appears when we imagine turning the clock back to the early Earth: before there were seeds, cells, or living ecosystems, how did the first systems capable of sustaining themselves and evolving arise?

Two questions are often confused here. Evolutionary biology investigates how living populations change and diversify across generations. Its conclusions are supported by converging lines of evidence, including genetics, fossils, comparative anatomy, and observed evolutionary processes. Natural selection is one important mechanism among several.

Research into the origin of life addresses a different problem: how nonliving chemistry might have given rise to the earliest living or life-like systems. Scientists investigate plausible pathways and environments, but there is not yet a universally accepted, complete reconstruction of everything that happened on the early Earth.

Uncertainty about the first emergence of life does not erase the evidence for evolution after life existed. And strong evidence for evolution does not mean every step in the origin of life has been explained.
Careful thinking begins by refusing to force two different questions into one answer.

At home, someone waters a plant on a windowsill and notices a new leaf opening between older ones. Knowing something about photosynthesis and cell division does not prevent that person from pausing to admire it. An explanation of how a process works need not extinguish wonder. Nor does wonder require us to reject an explanation.

sections.heading: 5. Consciousness: The Familiar Mystery
paragraphs: We wake in the morning and find ourselves inside a world of sensations. A headache hurts in a particular way. An old song brings back a memory that seems to carry the temperature of another year. A few words spoken in anger may remain vivid decades later.
These experiences are so ordinary that their strangeness can escape us. How do the activities of a nervous system relate to the felt quality of being someone?

Neuroscience has made substantial progress in understanding perception, attention, memory, and their relationships with brain activity. Researchers can investigate the neural conditions associated with different conscious states and compare competing theories. Yet how to give a complete account of subjective experience remains a matter of scientific and philosophical debate.

Saying that a question remains open does not mean nothing has been learned. Equally, measuring a neural process does not automatically settle every question about what an experience feels like from the inside.

The uncertainty should not be turned into a shortcut. We cannot conclude that consciousness must have a supernatural source merely because current explanations are incomplete. Nor should we pretend the debate has ended simply because brain activity is measurable.

Artificial intelligence adds another complication. A machine may hold a fluent conversation and perform demanding tasks. Those abilities do not, by themselves, establish that it has subjective experience. Assessing performance and deciding what would count as evidence of consciousness are different undertakings.

Meanwhile, the practical stakes are immediate. Imagine an older parent receiving a voice message that sounds exactly like a distant son or daughter. The familiar voice brings comfort—until the parent remembers that voices can now be imitated. Before acting on the message, someone needs to verify its source.

The urgent question in that moment is not whether the software has feelings. It is whether the person who made the recording had permission, whether the listener can identify a deception, and who is accountable if harm follows.
A machine can imitate the sound of concern. That does not excuse human beings from the duties of honesty and care.

sections.heading: 6. Foresight Is Not the Same as Prediction
paragraphs: We sometimes encounter an old saying that seems uncannily suited to the present. It is tempting to declare that someone centuries ago saw our future.

Perhaps the saying does contain a durable insight. Human lives repeatedly encounter ambition and restraint, growth and decline, power and its unintended consequences. A writer who noticed those patterns may still help us recognize them today.
But recognizing a recurring human dilemma is not the same as forecasting a specific event.

Take the familiar idea that extremes may give way to their opposites. As a warning against market euphoria, it can be useful. It does not tell an investor the date of the next decline or the size of the loss. Invoking the idea here is not a claim that this modern wording is a direct quotation from the original *Yijing*.

A prediction should expose itself to the possibility of failure. If someone says only that “markets will change,” almost any eventual outcome can be made to look like a success. If that person states a timeframe, conditions, and what would count as being wrong, others can evaluate the claim fairly.

The same care applies when a contemporary scientific discovery is compared with an ancient passage. We should ask when the passage was written, how it was understood before the discovery, and whether the resemblance survives a close reading rather than depending on a convenient translation.
These questions are not attacks on tradition. They protect worthwhile ideas from being buried under exaggerated claims.
Wisdom may help us ask better questions, recognize recurring dangers, and act with restraint. It does not become more valuable when we pretend it can predict what it cannot.

sections.heading: 7. When Technology Moves Faster Than Judgment
paragraphs: A century ago, a pocket-sized device offering instant conversation across oceans and access to vast libraries would have seemed extraordinary. Today we use such devices while waiting for a bus.
Technical progress can be astonishing. But speed is not direction.

A system that returns an answer in seconds may still be wrong. A tool that improves efficiency may also make unfair decisions at a greater scale. A product that performs well in a laboratory may behave differently when it enters the unpredictable circumstances of daily life.

A job applicant receives an automated rejection. There is no explanation and no clear way to appeal. Was a qualification missing, or did the system misunderstand a piece of work history? Across town, a patient learns that software has flagged a possible abnormality on a scan. The patient hopes the alert will help a clinician notice something important, but also needs to know that the result can be checked.
Neither person is asking only for faster computation. Each needs a process that allows questions, review, and responsible human response.

As AI systems enter hiring, education, healthcare support, and public communication, institutions and communities face questions that cannot be answered by accuracy scores alone. Where did the data come from? How are mistakes discovered? Who can challenge a decision? Who bears responsibility when a tool causes harm? Which decisions should never be left to an automated system acting alone?

The answers will differ by context and will need revision as evidence and practices change. A system used to suggest a movie is not subject to the same stakes as one used to assess a medical image. Rules, review procedures, and public expectations must reflect those differences.

That is precisely why ethical reflection and public debate remain essential. Their purpose is not to make innovation impossible. It is to ensure that, amid our fascination with what machines can do, we do not lose sight of the people affected by what machines do.

sections.heading: 8. Curiosity, Restraint, and the Courage to Say “I Don't Know”
paragraphs: As children, many of us wondered why the Moon seemed to follow us down the road. We stopped, and it appeared to stop. We ran, and there it was again, keeping pace above the rooftops.
An adult explained that the Moon was very far away. That answered part of the question. It also made room for another: why didn't it fall?

Growing older, we accumulate explanations. We also acquire schedules, responsibilities, and the habit of speaking with confidence. Somewhere along the way, “I don't know” can begin to sound like an admission of failure.
It is not.
There is no shame in recognizing the boundary of what we know. The greater risk is to cross that boundary without noticing and speak as though uncertainty had disappeared.

Science teaches us to discipline imagination with evidence. Philosophy asks us to examine the assumptions beneath our arguments. History reminds us how often certainty has served power, prejudice, or simple human vanity. None of these disciplines can remove uncertainty from life. Together, they can help us meet it more carefully.
“I don't know yet” need not end a conversation. It can begin an investigation: here is what the evidence shows; here is what remains unclear; here is what might change my mind.

We do not have to choose between respecting science and honoring the intellectual inheritance of earlier generations. Scientific claims should face scientific tests. Historical ideas deserve historical context. Questions of meaning and value require patient reasoning, attention to experience, and room for disagreement.

Years later, the boy who studied a galaxy on his father's phone may work with instruments his father could scarcely imagine. Perhaps he will remember not the distance his father looked up, but the moment his father paused before answering. He will know more about the universe. He will also encounter questions his father never thought to ask.
That will not mean the earlier generation failed. It will mean the search continued.

When science reaches the edge of the known, we do not need to write the answer in advance. We can say what the evidence supports, distinguish that from what we hope or suspect, and keep asking questions where the view remains uncertain.
**Respect science. Honor the thinkers of the past. Remain humble before the unknown.**
